Verdict: REVISE, narrowlyThe main argument is sound: the normalization terminates, component factorization is valid, the receiver-flux identities are exact, the five-edge promotion is feasible, the charge-two fixture has the stated final counts, and the elbow has a unique perfect matching and remains frozen under the allowed moves.There is one definite false statement at the stated generality: in §3,  $(6,4)$  need not have occupied degree four in every permitted feasible exterior. It has degree four in the charge-two fixture, and also whenever the initial configuration is single-terminal. The local move itself needs no repair.Two scope points should also be made explicit:The compensation reduction transports the signed scalar inequality appearing in the ledger, and hence the corresponding objective bound. It does not by itself transport a geometric assignment of donors to individual receivers.The conclusion about impossibility of a complete U/rotor cover depends on the cited source-subset exclusion having the required scope. The new proof establishes that the elbow’s endpoint and matching data cannot change.This is a mathematical audit of the supplied arguments and coordinates. I have not executed code or Lean, and I do not certify the reported checker or Lean coverage.1. Matching-exchange normalization: correctNecessary standing conventionThe argument uses
$$T\cap P=\varnothing,\qquad P=V(M),$$
in addition to the degree condition on  $T$ . This is the natural intended definition of the three labels—selected, endpoint, blank—but it should be explicit if it is not already a standing convention.The degree condition alone does not imply disjointness. For example, on the single edge  $uv$ , taking  $T=\{u\}$  and  $M=\{uv\}$  satisfies the stated degree condition, but promoting  $u$  would not increase  $|T|$ , so the claimed objective preservation would fail. This is a definition issue, not an objection under the intended disjoint-label model.Preservation and terminationFor a promotion bundle, let  $X$  be the promoted endpoints and  $Y$  their matching mates. If the bundle contains  $k$  edges, then
$$|X|=|Y|=k,\qquad X\cap Y=\varnothing,$$
and
$$T'=T\cup X,\qquad
P'=P\setminus(X\cup Y),\qquad
A'=A\setminus Y.$$
Consequently,
$$|T'|=|T|+k,\qquad |M'|=|M|-k,$$
so the objective is unchanged.Replacing the matching by a perfect matching of  $G[P]$  changes neither  $A$  nor the feasibility of the old selections. Every nonempty bundle decreases the matching size by at least one. Thus at most the original  $|M|$  bundle steps are possible.At termination, the absence of another permitted step is exactly the assertion that no perfect matching of the remaining induced endpoint graph admits a nonempty feasible promotion bundle. The proof does not need a canonical choice of matching or bundle, nor an efficient way of finding one.“Matching replacement” should allow choosing the current matching itself. With that convention, the statement that each promotion step is preceded by one matching replacement is harmless.Component factorizationThe factorization argument is correct, including the possible concern about selections outside the component.Let  $C$  be a component of  $G[P]$ . Every endpoint neighbor of an endpoint in  $C$  lies in  $C$ . Therefore, deletions of endpoint mates in another component cannot help a promoted vertex in  $C$  satisfy its degree bound. Its neighbors in the current selected set remain occupied throughout the step.Hence:Every perfect matching restricts to a perfect matching on each endpoint component.Restricting a feasible global bundle to the chosen edges in one component gives a feasible local bundle.A feasible local bundle extends by keeping the data in all other components unchanged.Old selected vertices create no obstruction to the restriction or extension: their occupied neighborhoods can only shrink.This remains true after previous promotions, when the current selected set includes vertices promoted earlier. All current selections are retained.Single-terminalityThe stated consequence is correct. If an endpoint  $x$  has occupied degree at most two, promoting  $x$  and deleting its current matching mate removes one occupied neighbor of  $x$ , leaving occupied degree at most one. Old selections remain feasible.Thus an exchange-terminal pair has no endpoint of occupied degree at most two and is single-terminal.The distinction from fixed-matching freezing is also correctly stated. A retained-mate certificate for one matching does not automatically certify another matching.The finite bipartite completeness assertion is consistent with the retained-mate rule. To see why, let  $F$  be its closure of frozen endpoints for a fixed matching. If  $F\ne P$ , choose a bipartition class containing an unfrozen endpoint and promote every unfrozen endpoint in that class. A retained endpoint neighbor of any such promoted vertex must be the mate of a frozen endpoint. Closure therefore says that the promoted vertex has at most one retained neighbor among those endpoints and the selections. This constructs a nonempty feasible bundle. Bipartiteness is doing real work in that argument.2. Receiver flux and nonreuse: correctUnder the supplied terminal receiver-partition hypothesis, equation (1) follows exactly from the whole-receiver identity.Fix an original component  $H$ . Because endpoint sets only decrease, every final endpoint belongs to a unique original component, and a final endpoint component cannot combine vertices from two original components.Since both endpoint configurations are single-terminal:The original physical receiver tiles have unique original owners.The descendant receivers are pairwise disjoint.Their union consists exactly of the tiles of  $R_H$  that still contain endpoints.Let  $k_H$  count the individual promotions descended from  $H$ . No promotion descended from another original component can introduce a selection into  $R_H$ : its promoted vertex was an original endpoint, and the original receivers are disjoint.Therefore the final counts throughout the original receiver are
$$|T_{\mathrm{final}}\cap R_H|=T_{R_H}+k_H,
\qquad
|P_{\mathrm{final}}\cap R_H|=|H|-2k_H.$$
Removing the freed tiles from this region gives
$$\sum_{K\prec H}T'_{R_K}
=
T_{R_H}+k_H-\sum_{Q\in F_H}t'_Q$$
and
$$\sum_{K\prec H}|R_K|
=
|R_H|-|F_H|.$$
Substitution yields
$$\begin{aligned}
\sum_{K\prec H}\rho'_K
&=
T_{R_H}+k_H-\sum_{Q\in F_H}t'_Q
+\frac{|H|-2k_H}{2}
-2\bigl(|R_H|-|F_H|\bigr)\\
&=
\rho_H+\sum_{Q\in F_H}(2-t'_Q).
\end{aligned}$$
This is precisely equation (1). The cancellation of the promotion count is valid.Nonnegativity and unique ownershipThe assertion  $t'_Q\le 2$  is correct. Any three vertices of a physical  $2\times2$  grid tile contain a selected vertex adjacent to two of the others. Thus three selections in one tile would violate feasibility.Consequently,
$$d'_Q=2-t'_Q\ge 0.$$
An original tile without endpoints cannot acquire an endpoint or a new selection: all new selections are original endpoints. It therefore remains unchanged. Every additional final no-endpoint tile belongs to exactly one  $F_H$ . Summing the regional identities gives
$$D'=D+\sum_H\sum_{Q\in F_H}d'_Q$$
and
$$D'-\sum_K\rho'_K=D-\sum_H\rho_H.$$
The nonreuse interpretation is accurate. A freed tile contributes the same increment to the final deficit and to the aggregate descendant charge. Its deficit cannot also be booked as an independent improvement in the signed compensation balance.No intermediate single-terminality assumption is needed. The counting uses the original and final receiver partitions and monotonicity of the endpoint set.One useful consequence makes the accounting especially clear:An original receiver with strictly positive charge cannot disappear completely under such a sequence ending in a single-terminal configuration.If it did, equation (1) would read
$$0=\rho_H+\sum_{Q\in F_H}d'_Q,$$
which is impossible when  $\rho_H>0$ .State the reduction’s target preciselyFor a single-terminal pair on a board with  $N$  physical tiles,
$$D-\sum_H\rho_H
=
2N-\bigl(|T|+|M|\bigr).$$
Indeed, the receivers and no-endpoint tiles partition the board, so this follows directly by expanding their definitions.Therefore the following implication is established:
$$\left[
D\ge\sum_H\rho_H
\text{ for every exchange-terminal pair}
\right]
\Longrightarrow
\left[
|T|+|M|\le 2N
\text{ for every feasible pair}
\right].$$
For an initially single-terminal pair, equation (2) also transfers the same signed compensation inequality directly.For an arbitrary initial pair, however, its endpoint receivers need not yet partition the physical tiles. The clean conclusion is the objective bound, obtained by normalization and objective preservation.I recommend replacing the final reduction sentence in §2 with:A signed compensation bound  $D\ge\sum_H\rho_H$  for every exchange-terminal representative implies the corresponding objective bound for every feasible pair. $$D-\sum_H\rho_H,$$
not an expression with  $\rho_H$  replaced by its positive part, and not a donor-assignment certificate. The lemma does not supply geometric information needed to transfer a particular assignment of physical donors to old receivers.3.
